articles.title: Pondering the biggest orb
articles.summary: The Vegas Sphere is the highest-resolution screen in the world and an entertainment phenomenon. It’s also a rare respite from our phones.
articles.body: The Sphere is the main character in Las Vegas right now. If you’re flying into the city from the right angle, half the plane sees it out the window and feels obligated to tell the other half what they’re witnessing. The woman on the flight next to me, who said she’d been to Vegas precisely 52 times, told the first-timer sitting in the window seat that the main thing he had to do this week was get into the Sphere. No problem, he said. He had U2 tickets. I, in the aisle seat, silently cursed him. I did not have U2 tickets. The night I was in Vegas, the available seats were $1,495 on Ticketmaster — and even those were gone by the time I checked again. The price was high but not surprising: you’re paying a Vegas premium, a Bono premium, and largest of all, a Sphere premium. Here are the salient specs of the Sphere, which opened this fall after five years and upward of $2 billion in construction. The building is 366 feet tall and 516 feet wide. The entire outside — which isn’t a sphere, if we’re going to get technical about it, it’s more like you chopped off the bottom of a cantaloupe to keep it from rolling off your counter — is a single display 580,000 square feet in size. The theater inside has 17,600 seats, 10,000 of which are wired to rumble and shake like a 4D Disney World ride. Another 2,400 people can stand around the stage in the bottom well of the arena, and currently, all 20,000 of those vacancies are filled a few nights a week by rabid U2 fans. I was in Vegas for other reasons, but I knew I couldn’t leave without somehow getting inside the Sphere. It is advertised as the biggest, highest-res, perhaps best screen on earth, a screen so big and so high-res, you don’t even notice it’s a screen. It is supposedly the future of entertainment, immersive and exciting enough to get you out of your house and your head out of your phone. The Sphere is an icon in the night sky, an ode to capitalism and our obsession with screens, a bunch of lights on a dome. It’s cool, futuristic, dystopian. I had to touch it. U2 wasn’t happening. But Sphere Entertainment had offered to comp me a $99 ticket to “The Sphere Experience,” which gets you an hour of time inside the Sphere’s lobby and a viewing of Postcard from Earth, a 50-minute tone poem slash tech demo created by the director Darren Aronofsky. (Sphere Entertainment is the company that runs the Sphere. It’s also a sister organization to MSG Entertainment, the conglomerate that owns and operates Radio City Music Hall, Madison Square Garden, and others. Both are run by James Dolan, who also owns New York’s Knicks and Rangers.) The irony of sitting in one of the world’s most expensive movie theaters to learn about the natural world didn’t bother me. I had to know how the screen worked, whether it worked. [Image: From two blocks away, the outside screen begins to reveal its secrets. As it peered over a parking lot and a bunch of construction materials, the Sphere looked like a single sparkling television. It was playing a swirling, colorful ad for the Sphere, which seemed redundant; everything the Sphere does, just by turning the electricity on, advertises the Sphere. From one block away, the orb started to shimmer a bit — I could see the pixels and that slight haze you get from a not-quite-sharp-enough display. From a few feet away, it’s not even a screen anymore. It’s more like a pointillist painting. The exterior of the Sphere is made up of lots of tiny round collections of LED “pucks.” Every puck has 48 tiny LED dots (I counted), and Sphere Entertainment says each dot can display 256 million colors (I didn’t count that). 1.4 million of those pucks (also didn’t count) cover the whole Sphere. Up close, the effect is roughly what you’d expect if you hung 57.6 million tiny Christmas lights around your large spherical house. It’s a lot of lights. The closest I got to the Sphere’s LEDs was about three feet. A combination of a metal barrier and a confused security guard, who didn’t seem sympathetic to my particular thirst for LED contact, kept me from getting any closer. So I scanned my ticket, went into the glowing blue atrium filled with holograms and talking robots and other things designed to make you feel vaguely good about the future of technology, purchased a $19 beer so I could test the automatic checkout scanners — for journalism! — and took my seat in Section 207, Row 8. The screen inside the theater is 160,000 square feet, and Sphere Entertainment proudly says it is 16,000 pixels by 16,000 pixels — the highest resolution in the world. This is apparently true and also entirely meaningless. At that size and resolution, the Sphere’s screen is about 1,600 pixels per square foot. The 50-inch Samsung HG50NE477SF Hospitality TV in my hotel room, by contrast, has a resolution of 1,920 by 1,080 pixels and measures roughly 7.405 square feet, which adds up to 280,027 pixels per square foot. If we’re just measuring pixel density, sitting really close to my HG50NE477SF resoundingly defeats trekking two miles and dropping a Benjamin to gaze upon the Sphere. From my seat in 207, roughly in the center of the theater, I received no clues about the makeup of the enormous screen in front of, above, next to, and even slightly behind me. But since The Sphere Experience only sells a portion of the seats in the theater for each show, Section 211, over by the wall, was wide open. Section 211 is so far to the side that it’d be like trying to watch a movie from the theater’s bathroom, but it has one thing going for it: the screen is just right there. [Image: Up close, the Sphere’s screen is... is it even a screen at all? I looked closely at the screen. I touched the screen. Though I’m not even sure “screen” is the right word. The Sphere’s screen is more like a chain mail of light bulbs. It’s a pixel mesh. It’s a rigid, thin, see-through structure of endless rows of tiny LED dots. This design leaves the display thin enough to allow the Sphere’s 1,600 speaker panels to blast spatial audio through the screen without any visible speakers in the auditorium. It’s also a flexible enough structure to wrap up the ceiling and around the walls. It’s a screen deconstructed, reduced only to the parts that matter: the pixels. If you’re looking for the pixels, you’ll see them. I definitely saw them. There was a dead one down toward the bottom left side of the Sphere — I saw that one for sure. But a few minutes into Postcard from Earth, back in my centrally placed seat in 207, I stopped paying attention. The pixel density pretty quickly gives way to the vibes. The movie starts in the same theater-sized rectangular display that was swirling with color before the show started, and it stays there long enough that the group of four 20-something dudes behind me started to wonder if this was all there was to the Sphere. But after some melodramatic introductions to the idea of Earth, in case you’ve never heard of the planet, the real show begins. The camera zooms into the pale blue dot, and the screen expands. And expands. And expands. A minute later, when we were suddenly surrounded by and hurtling through snowy mountains, the dudes abided, sipping their drinks and loudly crinkling some snacks I couldn’t identify but couldn’t stop hearing. “Whoa,” one of them said. “Okay, this is sick.” He’s not wrong; the Sphere is a sick place to see a movie. You don’t so much as watch something in the Sphere as you temporarily move into its universe. It makes anything, even this knockoff Planet Earth episode, feel grand and visceral. For the rest of Postcard from Earth, we, the audience, were subjected to a series of gorgeous vignettes accompanied by melodramatic narration that is — spoiler alert! — very concerned about climate change. A spider jumped toward the screen, and literally thousands of people screamed and jumped. An enormous elephant padded by, hundreds of feet tall, and our chairs rumbled with every footprint. When we flew through the mountains, a wind blew in our faces. When the camera tipped over a cliff’s edge down into a canyon, one of the dudes grabbed onto his armrests and said to his friend, “Yo, this is like a roller coaster!” If you’ve ever been to a planetarium or on the Soarin’ ride at Epcot, you have an idea of what it’s like to be in the Sphere, with video so big and so encompassing that it feels like you’re moving with the camera. The Sphere is that, only much more so, which comes with some tricky new considerations. Aronofsky shot the film on a custom 18K camera developed specifically for the Sphere’s dimensions and told The Hollywood Reporter that one of the hardest parts of the process, other than managing the half-petabyte of footage they shot, was “how to make audiences feel comfortable with their peripheral vision filled with imagery.” The Sphere has rooms just outside the theater for anyone whose senses are overwhelmed by the experience, and I wasn’t the only person who looked down at my lap during one especially flashing-lights-filled part of Postcard from Earth. But the Sphere is not meant to be comfortable. It is meant to blow your mind. That is the whole reason it exists, its whole competitive advantage over not just other concert venues and movie theaters but its true adversary: your smartphone. Personally, I’ve developed a nasty habit the last few years of putting on a movie “I really want to see” and then looking at my phone through the whole thing. At least for one night, Postcard from Earth cured me of that impulse. By the end of the film’s runtime, I’d developed a theory of the Sphere. A Sphere theory. A Spheory. Here it is: the Sphere is the opposite of TikTok. We live in a time filled with scrolling, in which so much of our lives is about the activity of swiping up and down and left and right, moving between things, constantly remixing and interacting and sharing. Hardly anything in modern entertainment just happens to us anymore; we demand to always be involved. But the Sphere happens to you, and it happens in such a huge, multisensory, occasionally discombobulating way that it demands your full attention. The experience may be different at a concert, which is, by design, more participatory. You sing, you dance, you take videos you’ll never watch again. U2 fans have certainly posted enough videos to make it clear that the Sphere’s screen is, in addition to everything else, eminently shareable. But when it wants to, it can be immersive unlike anything else I’ve ever seen. Marco Brambilla, an artist who has worked with immersive technology for years and designed part of U2’s concert experience, tells me that the most exciting thing about the Sphere was having this kind of fully embracing experience with no headset required. [Media: At the same time, though, it is inescapably true that while I was in Las Vegas — a city filled with epic architecture and packed full of people from all over the world, a few hours away from the Grand Canyon, down the road from the Hoover Dam and the Red Rock Canyon and so many other gorgeous natural sights — the only thing that got me looking up from my phone was 160,000 feet of lights and some fake wind. One of the things you hear people talk about in the U2 concerts is a moment where the Sphere’s picture changes, and it shows… the Vegas skyline from the exact perspective of the Sphere. A video of the Vegas skyline. “It’s like the screen went away!” people say, staring at the screen. Think about it too long, and it all gets pretty bleak. But whatever, it’s 2023. Screens rule everything around me. That’s what I came to understand about the Sphere: it’s not the ideal solution to all our antisocial screen-based lifestyle woes, but it’s probably the most effective one. The Sphere posits that the only cure to Too Much Screen is Way More Screen. In the war between the real world and the shining lights, the lights already won. The only way to sell tickets is to promise more and better lights. Right now, the Sphere is a building, but pretty soon, the Sphere might be a new genre of entertainment. The company is pushing to build a Sphere in London, though it has been met with backlash from locals who would rather not have a giant glowing ball right outside their windows day and night. (It promised blackout curtains for nearby Vegas residents, but those folks are also likely a bit more used to light pollution than your average Londoner.) There’s already a smaller Sphere in Burbank, California, which is the home of Sphere Studios and technical development for the huge domes. Dolan, the big boss and the original artist behind the “circle with a stick person inside” sketch that eventually became the Sphere, has said he wants Spheres all over the world. With great Sphere comes great challenges, though. A typical movie would look, sound, and feel awful on that large wraparound screen, and I wouldn’t pay $100 to come back, sit with my $19 beer, and watch Wonka on a tiny rectangular portion of the screen. U2 spent months working with Brambilla and many other artists to properly visualize its concert. The Sphere is a new kind of venue that needs an entirely new kind of entertainment, and that’s even harder to create than a giant wall of pixels. But I’d go again. For 50 consecutive minutes, the Sphere consumed my universe. I didn’t touch my phone once, and I even forgot all about my $19 beer. It was just me, the dudes, a few thousand of our friends, 1,600 speakers, and 25.6 million lights. It was all we could do to keep up. In a world consumed by documenting, participating, posting, streaming, and sharing, there simply is no second screen Sphere experience. There is no second screen. There is only the Sphere. Update Dec. 21, 10:45am: Updated to clarify the ownership structure of the Sphere, which is run by Sphere Entertainment.

articles.title: The gen AI Kool-Aid tastes like eugenics
articles.summary: Ghost in the Machine — out on Kinema March 26th — director Valeria Veatch speaks with The Verge about gen AI’s roots in eugenics.
articles.body: Like many people, director Valerie Veatch was intrigued when OpenAI first released its Sora text-to-video generative AI model to the public in 2024. Though she didn’t fully understand the technology, she was curious about what it could do, and she saw that other artists were building online communities to share their new AI creations. The hope of connecting with people drew Veatch into the AI space, but once she was there, she was shocked to see how often the technology would generate images dripping with racism and sexism. Veatch was even more unsettled by the way her new AI-enthusiast peers did not seem to care that the machine they rallied around spewed out hateful, bigoted garbage without being explicitly prompted to do so. The bizarre situation drove Veatch away from her early experimentation with gen AI. But it also inspired her to make Ghost in the Machine, a new documentary about the technologies and schools of thought that laid the groundwork for gen AI’s existence. Instead of focusing on the potential (if highly improbable) benefits to society that gen AI accelerationists swear are just around the corner, Ghost in the Machine explores the technology’s history to explain why it works the way it does now. When I recently spoke with Veatch about the film, she told me that she wanted to chronicle gen AI’s genesis to give people a clear view of the very intense cycle of industry hype we’re currently living through. First, however, she had to cut through AI firms’ purposeful obfuscation of the entire concept. “In order to use the phrase ‘artificial intelligence,’ we have to know what the fuck that phrase means,” Veatch told me over a video call. “The truth is, it doesn’t mean anything; it’s a marketing term and always has been. It’s a completely misleading, stupid phrase that has taken on its own cultural meaning, and I think being really clear about the words we use and the meaning of those words is essential.” [Media: As Ghost in the Machine repeatedly stresses, “artificial intelligence” was originally coined in 1956 by computer scientist John McCarthy when he was trying to secure more funding for his projects. But the documentary presents the term’s coinage as just one of many important points on a timeline that actually begins in Victorian-era England with the birth of eugenics. In addition to being Charles Darwin’s cousin, Francis Galton was the originator of eugenics — the racist and discredited belief that humanity can be improved through the systemic elimination of “inferior” (read: non-white) races. While Galton definitely made some useful contributions to academia, in our interview, Veatch explained that it is important to not minimize the fact that his deeply held white supremacist beliefs informed the era’s social sciences. Galton and his fellow eugenicist / protegee Karl Pearson were not directly involved in the development of early computational machines. But Galton’s foundational work with multidimensional modeling — a technique he used while measuring the attractiveness of African and European women — shaped Pearson’s thinking as he developed statistical tools like logistic regression, which is one of the fundamental components of modern machine learning. Galton Pearson helped normalize the idea that people of various races were fundamentally different in quantifiable ways. This kind of racist thinking is what led to Galton and his peers believing that human intelligence could be measured, and that human brains function very much like machines. That jump, Veatch says, played a major role in selling the public on the fantastical idea of artificial intelligence. “What was really surprising to me during my initial dive into all of this was how, when you look at the question of superintelligence as a documentarian or journalist, it doesn’t take long before you smack your forehead into the low doorframe of race science because it’s baked into this technology,” Veatch said, explaining that these concepts are “soaked” in eugenic thinking. Rather than trying to disprove the idea that gen AI models produce hateful ideology because they’ve been trained on it (a concept commonly known as “GIGO” — garbage in, garbage out), Ghost in the Machine uses its historical analysis to explain why the companies building this technology seem so disinterested in addressing its present-day issues. This historical context helped Veatch make sense of some of her own troubling experiences with gen AI, back when she was playing around with an early version of Sora in an artists’ Slack. Veatch remembers the group as being a friendly, welcoming place right up until another member — a woman of color — began voicing concerns about the way the model whitewashed her every time she prompted it to generate images based on photos of herself. “It kept her braids and it kept her fashion, but she was prompting herself into an art gallery, which the program understood to be a ‘white space,’” Veatch explained. “My reaction was ‘what the fuck,’ and I tried explaining to the group how this was really a problem with the software itself.” No one else in the group engaged with her post. “This was a Slack where, normally, there are always like dozens of screaming koala emoji reactions on every post. But this time, there was nothing.” [Image: Veatch took it upon herself to get in contact with OpenAI directly to alert the company about “how racist, sexist, and misogynistic the outputs [she] was seeing were — outputs where women would start growing extra tits and twerking after like two rounds of generating a scene.” Veatch thought OpenAI would see this as a critical bug worth fixing before encouraging more people to adopt Sora into their lives; instead the company brushed her concerns aside. “The feedback I got was basically, ‘This is very cringe to be bringing up; there’s nothing we can do to change it,’” Veatch recalled. That situation lit a fire within Veatch to learn about why so many different forms of generative intelligence consistently behave in such ugly, troublesome ways. At first, she didn’t really think that having Zoom calls with the authors of white papers about the technology could be turned into a compelling documentary, but that changed as she began to see a clear line from Galton’s eugenic statistics work to modern gen AI outfits. The voices featured in Ghost in the Machine — a blend of AI researchers, historians, and critical theorists — make a compelling case that basically every facet of the AI space has been profoundly influenced by its historical connections to fields of science built to support discriminatory world views. When I asked Veatch if she had ever been interested in speaking directly with the heads of the companies Ghost in the Machine takes to task, she laughed. Getting that kind of access, she said, would require her to go through all kinds of ideological gymnastics and make compromises that would make her film complicit in gen AI’s harms. “There’s the idea, you know, these people won’t trust just anyone,” Veatch said. “Yeah, no shit, and I certainly hope they wouldn’t trust me. I don’t want them in the film and they already speak enough to the media. Am I going to hug Sam Altman on camera? Is that a truthful film about this technology? That’s propaganda.” Ghost in the Machine will be available to stream via Kinema from March 26th to March 28th before it airs on PBS some time this fall. Correction, March 21st: An earlier version of this story used the phrase “logical regression” when “logistic regression” is correct.

articles.title: “Practical Magic 2 ”breaks the spell “Spider-Man ”and “The Odyssey ”held over the box office, but fails to conjure a profit
articles.summary: The witchy sequel recouped only $46 million of its estimated $75 million budget — but will it find lasting power at the box office?
articles.body:
Practical Magic 2 is the new queen in town after ousting both The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day from their long-held spots at the top of the box office.

Warner Bros.' sequel to the 1998 classic easily overtook its competitors this weekend, but $46 million globally isn't a great opening take for a film that cost $75 million to produce.

Next week, Zach Cregger's Resident Evil will attempt to claw its way to the top spot.

After nine weeks of undisputed dominance, The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day have fallen to a witchy new foe. But Practical Magic 2 's spell over the box office may not have been cast to last.

Director Susanne Bier and co-writers Akiva Goldsman, Georgia Pritchett, and Kelly Marcel's spellbinding sequel to the 1998 classic directed by Griffin Dunne and written by Goldsman, Robin Swicord, and Adam Brooks conjured up $30 million domestically and $46 million globally this week, per box office tracker Rentrak.

Those sums were more than enough to knock Matt Damon's Odysseus and Tom Holland's Spidey down a peg, securing the witchy Owens women, led by Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock , a No. 1 film at home and abroad. That's a win for Warner Bros., which took a gamble on the sequel nearly 30 years in the making. But the studio may not be viewing its odds so favorably.

Sure, The Odyssey fell to No. 3 with $7.4 million domestically and $34.4 million around the world. But that's after an astonishing nine weeks in theaters. The star-studded adaptation of Homer's seafaring epic currently boasts over $600 million in the former market, placing it second behind Brand New Day in the overall domestic leaderboard for 2026, and a whopping $1.68 billion in the latter market — ditto on the global rankings.

As for Brand New Day , Holland's fourth outing as the web-slinger has shattered records virtually every week since its early August opening. The film added $8.4 million domestically and $27.4 million globally this weekend, making for $935.1 million overall in the former market and $2.45 billion in the latter.

Bier, Warners, and even Kidman and Bullock (who serve as producers) certainly didn't expect their sister witches to seriously contend with a behemoth IP like Spider-Man. But $46 million is a worrying start for a film made on an estimated $75 million budget, especially considering that the cost of the film's marketing blitz isn't factored into that estimate.

But all may not be lost for Practical Magic 2 . It's sure to recoup at least its budget within the next couple weeks, and as Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak's Head of Marketplace Trends, noted in a Sunday interview with AP, "It's not necessarily about that opening weekend... Weekend two will tell the tale, no question about it." Practical Magic 2 is "the kind of movie that you can build an evening at the movie theater around with your friends," one that may find a lasting place at the movieplex.

Elsewhere on the weekend's box office leaderboards, the independent Christian outfit Angel Studios misfired with Runner , a thriller starring Alan Ritchson as a former soldier racing to save a child's life as a drug cartel closes in. The film opened to $6.6 million domestically atop a budget estimated between $35-45 million.

Coyote vs. Acme , however, once seen as little more than a victim of studio cruelty , has proven an enduring hit, adding another $6.2 million to its domestic coffers, which now reach $47.7 million.

Get your daily dose of entertainment news, celebrity updates, and what to watch with our EW Dispatch newsletter .

Next week, Zach Cregger returns just over a year after his bizarro Weapons became a centerpiece of the 2025 horror conversation. His take on Resident Evil will play against Ethan Hawke's historical drama The Weight — as well as Practical Magic 2 , Brand New Day , and The Odyssey , of course, for the box office gold.

articles.title: 'Musk' film is almost four hours long, engrossing and terrifying. What to know.
articles.summary: The documentary paints the tech trillionaire as a power-hungry megalomaniacal conman with a god complex. Musk accuses filmmaker Alex Gibney of compiling "hit...
articles.body:
TORONTO — Nearly four hours with Elon Musk.

The filmmaker, once described by Esquire as "becoming the most important documentarian of our time," has tackled Enron, Eliot Spitzer, Vladimir Putin and Elizabeth Holmes. Now, he's turned his eyes to the richest man in the history of the world.

Your weekly guide to culture, entertainment, and what everyone is talking about. Sign up for free

The 3-hour-and-45-minute "Musk" (plus a 10-minute intermission) hits theaters on Oct. 16, but it's already causing a stir.

The documentary, which spans from his early Silicon Valley days through his Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) dalliances and Twitter acquisition to his ascent to becoming the world's first trillionaire, paints Musk as an emotionally unstable grifter with more power and influence than perhaps any other human who has ever lived.

Gibney pulls no punches, neither in the documentary nor in interviews about it, in which he's called Musk's power and influence "extremely dangerous to world democracy."

"What I discovered was that the story of Musk was not a new tech story," Gibney told reporters in a news conference at the Venice Film Fest earlier this month, adding that it's "really the story of an old wine in a new bottle. His story turns out to be the story of the confidence man, the stock pumper. His wealth and power comes from inflated stock, and so I had told that story before with Enron and with Elizabeth Holmes, and so it was a story that was oddly familiar to me."

As you might expect, Musk is not exactly flattered by the depiction.

"Gibney just assembled a hit list of people who either have an axe to grind or don't even know me (but still have an axe to grind)," he tweeted last week. "He has ZERO integrity. Horrible human."

Alex Spiro, Musk's attorney, sent Gibney's Jigsaw Productions a letter threatening to file a defamation suit, according to the Hollywood Reporter . The claims center on a text exchange between Musk and Ashley St. Clair, a former girlfriend with whom he has a child, which is presented in the film.

In the exchange, Musk tells St. Clair he's feeling more optimistic about the 2024 election, in which he supported President Donald Trump, because "tomorrow we unleash the anomaly in the matrix." He adds, "I have over 10 thousand lasers in space right now."

I caught "Musk" at a 9 a.m. press and market screening at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday. There's a tremendous amount to parse, but here are a few immediate takeaways.

Sunday's screening began at 9 a.m. and let out at 1 p.m. If I hadn't looked at a clock, I might have guessed about two hours had passed.

Gibney's film moves fluidly, though. It helps that it's deeply comprehensive, beginning with Musk co-founding Zip2 in 1995 and running through the Defense Department's embrace of Grok earlier this summer.

The movie doesn't hit the audience with any atom bombs of new information. Instead, it weaves all the random strings of Musk's empire and life with which you likely have a vague familiarity — Tesla, SpaceX, his extreme pronatalism, his shifting politics, Grok, Twitter, DOGE, Starlink — into a stark character study of a man who may have once been a true believer in futurism and helping humanity.

But who, as presented by the documentary, has become a power-hungry megalomaniacal con man with a god complex.

The movie begins with Musk discussing simulation theory, the idea that we're all actually living in a computer simulation. To explain why he believes this could be true, he points to the rapid advancement of video games from Pong to hyperrealistic, dynamic massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs) that thousands of people around the globe play simultaneously. If we can make that leap in 50 years, he reasons, how could we not have already reached a point of creating a true simulation of life?

When the documentary was first announced, before Gibney approached Musk for an interview, the tech titan tweeted , "Gibney is a douche." You can safely assume he does not participate in the film.

As a work-around, Gibney turned to Musk's interest in the simulation theory, feeding AI every public statement Musk has made and then generating an uncanny, eerie, animated digital avatar of Musk to speak the very words fed into it.

Gibney takes things further, using a video game motif throughout the movie (a nod to Musk's adoration of gaming). When Musk is making massive cuts throughout the federal government as the head of DOGE, for example, the movie turns into a first-person shooter video game in which Musk yields an animated chainsaw.

The most emotionally fraught aspects of the film come during interviews with Musk's former romantic partners.

His first wife, Justine Musk, with whom he had six children, said she learned the term "gaslighting" through their relationship.

Their first child, Nevada, died of sudden infant death syndrome 10 weeks after birth. In November 2022, Musk tweeted , "My firstborn child died in my arms. I felt his last heartbeat."

But Justine says that she, in fact, was holding Nevada.

In a shaky voice, Justine says it wasn't uncommon for the Musk to bend reality and present it as truth, to criticize her, to try to control her. While dancing on their wedding night, Musk told her, "I am the alpha in this relationship."

"He would invent the arena of the conversation and knock you out of it," she says, adding that their marriage was "war, peace, war, peace."

"I am your wife, not your employee," she recalls telling him again and again. Then, she recalls his response: "If you were my employee, I would fire you."

According to St. Clair, the former MAGA influencer with whom Musk has a child, Musk tries desperately to keep his private life private. Musk offered her $15 million and $100,000 a month for 21 years to sign a nondisclosure agreement requiring her not to share the paternity of her son Romulus with anyone except Romulus himself.

Musk first approached her via Twitter, which she says is not unusual for him. She says she's since heard from many other young women whom Musk approached on Twitter with the offer to donate his sperm to them in his ardent pronatalist attempt to populate the world with his offspring.

"It's like a Gatling gun of sperm in his DMs," she says.

The musician Grimes, with whom he shares three children, also briefly appears in the documentary. While they were having their second child together, Musk secretly had twins with colleague Shivon Zilis via in vitro fertilization.

Grimes and Musk later had a custody battle over their three children, whom Grimes claimed he took from her.

One of Musk's goals, the documentary posits, is to have as many children as possible. He texted St. Clair he wants to create "a legion of children before the civil war."

In a voice-over, Gibney says there are 14 known children of Musk's but likely many more. Musk has built a compound in Austin for the children and their mothers.

His thinking, according to tech journalist Kara Swisher: "I have superior genes, and I need to procreate."

Musk's parents also appear in the documentary. His father Errol, it should be noted, told the Sun in 2022 that "the only thing we are on Earth for is to reproduce." He was defending having a second child with his stepdaughter. (You read that correctly.) Errol describes his son's childhood as one rife with bullying and beatdowns.

His mother, Maye, meanwhile describes a chaotic household in which Errol would tell her three times a day how stupid and ugly she was, before occasionally beating her.

One of Gibney's tricks as a filmmaker is showing how Musk presents his businesses and accomplishments before showing the reality of them.

"He was a skilled inventor of his own value," Gibney says in voice-over.

One of the film's lengthier passages focuses on Tesla, showing several incongruities between public statement and actual fact.

During one presentation, Musk claims to have solved the biggest hurdle electric cars face — a limited battery life — by creating stations that quickly swap out the thousand-plus-pound battery for another. The film then cuts to the only actual station that was ever built, a pilot one in Harris Ranch, California.

Gibney's main interest in Tesla, though, is Musk's frequent claims that the cars could simply drive themselves. He shows multiple clips of Musk saying you can play video games or take a nap and let the car drive. He shows the famous "Paint It Black" video, which supposedly demonstrated this technology, only to have a former Tesla engineer admit he was in the car writing code on the fly to make it work — and the video still required editing.

To save money, the film adds, Tesla used cameras instead of the advanced lidar sensors to guide the autopilot. The film then presents gut-wrenching footage of fatal crashes, which it alleges were caused by autopilot.

So far, faulty autopilot has allegedly caused more than 60 deaths. Details of most cases are not known, as Tesla settled with most of the victims' families.

Throughout the movie, we watch as Musk reverses previously held positions when it can benefit him, such as his flip from stark AI skeptic who believes it will exterminate humanity (if it doesn't keep us around as pets) to one of the loudest pro-AI voices out there who has integrated his chatbot Grok into the U.S. military.

For most of his time on the public stage, Musk was nonpolitical. In one clip, he says he's socially liberal and economically in the center. Then came the pandemic.

"Covid is when some switch got flipped in his brain," says neuroscientist and podcaster Sam Harris, who was close with Musk until they fell out after Musk began tweeting that "the coronavirus panic is dumb."

Musk became one of the loudest critics of lockdown, reopening a Tesla factory in Alameda County despite its lockdown rules. Roughly 450 cases of covid-19 were subsequently reported.

Meanwhile, the government opened several investigations into Musk and his companies. The documentary argues this was the real reason behind his embrace of Trump: to shut those down.

"If Kamala Harris wins, his goose is cooked," Swisher says. "His only choice was helping Trump and Trump would leave him alone."

Or, as Tucker Carlson told him before the election : "If he loses, man, you're f---ed, dude."

"If he loses, I'm f---ed," Musk responds.

This barely scrapes the surface of "Musk," a triumphant work of documentary that seeks to answer a question St. Clair poses: "What is Elon actually building? What are his goals?"

There's Twitter/X. There's SpaceX. There's DOGE. There's destruction of the United States Agency for International Development and the global fallout. There's lawsuits claiming Grok is used to create child porn. There's Starlink. There's the way it's all interconnected.

Gibney doesn't end with a conclusion, instead allowing the audience to decide for themselves what to make of this almost mythical figure.

For her part, though, St. Clair has decided:

articles.title: 'Levo cada um no meu coração', diz Gaby Amarantos na Parada LGBT | G1
articles.standfirst: Cantora paraense se apresentou no encerramento da 20ª Parada do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+, nesse domingo (13), em Rio Branco. Cerca de 10 mil pessoas participaram do circuito e do show.
articles.summary: Cantora paraense se apresentou no encerramento da 20ª Parada do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+, nesse domingo (13), em Rio Branco. Cerca de 10 mil pessoas participaram do circuito e do show.
articles.body:
🏳‍🌈✨ Com brilho, cores vibrantes, trio elétrico e muita música, a 20ª Parada do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+ levou o público para as ruas da capital acreana nesse domingo (13). A programação terminou em frente ao Palácio Rio Branco , no Centro da cidade, com o show da cantora paraense Gaby Amarantos, atração principal do evento.

Segundo a organização, cerca de 10 mil pessoas participaram do circuito e acompanharam a apresentação da artista . A concentração começou às 15h no Skate Park, no Parque da Maternidade . De lá, os participantes seguiram pelas avenidas Ceará, Brasil e Getúlio Vargas.

Gaby Amarantos voltou ao Acre após 16 anos e falou sobre a emoção de reencontrar o público durante o show. A cantora destacou as experiências que viveu no estado e agradeceu pelo carinho recebido.

“O momento que eu mais estava esperando era estar aqui com vocês, cantando e celebrando. Fiz amigos que vou levar para sempre no meu coração, vivi experiências da floresta que me completaram pra sempre, recebi amor, dei amor, dei carinho e levo cada um de vocês no meu coração . Muito obrigada”, disse Gaby.

A artista esteve em Rio Branco pela última vez em dezembro de 2010 , quando se apresentou no Festival Varadouro. Na época, Gaby estava em ascensão nacional com o hit “Ex Mai Love”, que depois virou tema da novela “Cheias de Charme”, em 2012.

Gaby Amarantos se apresenta na 20ª Parada do Orgulho LGBT+ em Rio Branco — Foto: Renato Menezes/g1

Este ano o evento teve como tema “Orgulho que movimenta o Acre: Cultura, Turismo, Diversidade e Empreendedorismo” . A proposta foi destacar a diversidade e discutir temas ligados à cultura, ao turismo, à geração de renda e ao empreendedorismo da população LGBTQIAPN+.

A 20ª Parada teve mudança no trajeto em relação às edições anteriores. O novo percurso foi anunciado na quinta-feira (10) , após reunião entre os organizadores e representantes da Secretaria de Estado de Justiça e Segurança Pública (Sejusp) e do Departamento Estadual de Trânsito (Detran).

O esquema de segurança contou com policiais militares, agentes do Detran, bombeiros, servidores da RBTrans e profissionais de segurança privada. Segundo a organização, a mudança levou em conta questões de segurança, mobilidade urbana e acesso dos serviços de saúde.

Veja FOTOS da 20ª Parada do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+ no Acre

A edição deste ano marcou a retomada do desfile da Parada do Orgulho LGBTQIAPN+ de Rio Branco após uma série de adiamentos. Em 2025, o evento não ocorreu nas datas inicialmente previstas, 7 de dezembro e depois 17 de maio deste ano.

Ao g1 , o ativista Germano Marino explicou que, embora o desfile tradicional não tenha acontecido nas datas previstas, a programação seguiu com o Circuito Acreano da Diversidade, formado por diferentes atividades.

A última Parada do Orgulho LGBT+ em Rio Branco havia acontecido em dezembro de 2024 e reuniu cerca de 7 mil pessoas, segundo a organização.

20ª Parada do Orgulho LGBT+ reuniu milhares de pessoas em Rio Branco — Foto: Renato Menezes/g1

articles.title: Mormaço Cultural 2026: Rolê Gastronômico tem pratos em Boa Vista | G1
articles.standfirst: 'Rolê Gastronômico' reúne restaurantes com pratos especiais inspirados na culinária regional até 20 de setembro. Público pode participar do 'passaporte premiado' e trocar três carimbos por um brinde.
articles.summary: O Rolê Gastronômico do Mormaço Cultural 2026 reúne restaurantes de Boa Vista com pratos regionais e brindes para o público até 20 de setembro.
articles.body:
Comidas servidas no 'Rolê Gastronômico' do Festival Mormaço 2026 — Foto: Semuc/Divulgação

A programação do Festival Mormaço Cultural 2026 continua nesta semana com o "Rolê Gastronômico", que reúne restaurantes de Boa Vista com nove pratos inspirados na culinária regional . A lista inclui opções como peixe com geleia de açaí , camarão com banana frita e carne de sol com queijo coalho (veja detalhadamente mais abaixo).

O Mormaço chegou à 5ª edição neste ano. A programação inclui shows nacionais e locais, peças teatrais, atrações infantis, atividades culturais e iniciativas sobre a culinária local, como o "Rolê Gastronômico". Até o dia 20 de setembro, os restaurantes participantes oferecem pratos especiais.

Os preços variam conforme o estabelecimento, o tamanho ou quantidade servida. Há opções a partir de R$ 48,90. Confira os pratos:

O prato leva camarões crocantes envolvidos com banana frita, acompanhados de geleia de açaí com pimenta. A opção custa R$ 69,90 e é vendido no Bar da Brahma , localizado na avenida Ville Roy, 2092, bairro Caçari, na zona Leste.

O prato é feito com arroz, feijão, ovo, legumes, ervas, bacon, calabresa, maminha fatiada e molho ferrugem. O preço é de R$ 99,90 o quilo e está disponível no restaurante Yano Cozinha , localizado na avenida Glaycon de Paiva, 1240, bairro Mecejana, zona Oeste.

A receita tem dourado ao molho de moqueca com leite de coco, acompanhado de arroz branco e farofa de piracuí. O preço é de R$ 114,90 o quilo no Riu Restaurante , localizado na rua Floriano Peixoto, 545, no Centro de Boa Vista.

A pizza tem molho de tomate, queijo muçarela, carne de sol desfiada, queijo coalho, pimenta-biquinho, tomate e orégano. A massa é feita com batata-doce. A opção custa R$ 89 na versão pequena, R$ 106 na média, R$ 136 na grande e R$ 178 na família e está disponível na pizzaria Ki Legal , localizado na rua Laura Pinheiro Maia, 369, Pintolândia, zona Oeste.

O prato é feito com galeto assado na brasa, acompanhado de arroz carreteiro, polenta, macarrão ao alho e óleo e molho de ervas. Custa R$ 48,90 para uma pessoa e R$ 78,90 para duas pessoas. É vendido na Casa Roraima Galeteria , localizado na avenida Santos Dumont, 1952, bairro 31 de Março , zona Leste.

A receita combina filé de dourado ao molho de camarão, camarão, ovo e batata cozidos, arroz refogado com açafrão, farofa de banana-da-terra e batata sautê. O prato custa R$ 75 e está disponível no Bar e Restaurante do Dedinho , rua Manoel Barbosa de Araújo, 146, no 31 de Março, na zona Leste.

O prato é composto por filé de dourado assado no forno, risoto de pimenta, pirão de farinha branca e farofa panko, acompanhado de pimenta e limão. A opção custa R$ 56 e é vendida no Meu Buteco , localizado na rua Eduardo Ribeiro, 233, São Francisco, zona Leste.

O restaurante preparou filé de peixe recheado com queijo e camarão, servido ao molho de camarão. O prato acompanha arroz branco, farofa e salada. A porção custa R$ 140, serve três pessoas e está disponível Restaurante Tropical do Norte, na rua Pedro Rodrigues, 174, Centro.

Este ano, o evento oferece o Passaporte Premiado , em que o público que visitar os restaurantes participantes pode juntar três carimbos de estabelecimentos diferentes e trocar o passaporte por um brinde. A troca ocorre nos dias 18, 19 e 20 de setembro, das 18h às 22h, no Parque do Rio Branco.

Este ano, o festival terá shows nacionais de Seu Jorge , Amado Batista , Cidade Negra , Fresno, Kevin O Chris , Melody , Ferrugem , Dennis , Filipe Ret e Cat Dealers .

articles.title: Festival Dabacuri reúne boi-bumbá e danças em Manaus nos dias 18 e 19 de setembro | G1
articles.standfirst: Evento arrecada alimentos para abrigos infantis e terá feira gastronômica com comidas regionais.
articles.summary: Evento arrecada alimentos para abrigos infantis e terá feira gastronômica com comidas regionais.
articles.body:
Festival Dabacuri acontece nos dias 18 e 19 de setembro, na unidade Jorge Deixeira do SEST SENAT. — Foto: Divulgação/SEST SENAT - Amazonas

O Festival Dabacuri, promovido pelo Serviço Social do Transporte e pelo Serviço Nacional de Aprendizagem do Transporte (Sest Senat), será realizado nos dias 18 e 19 de setembro, na unidade Jorge Teixeira, na Avenida Autaz Mirim, zona Leste de Manaus. A programação inclui apresentações de boi-bumbá, dança de salão, quadrilha, ciranda, zumba e pagode.

A entrada será feita com a doação de 1 kg de alimento não perecível. Os itens arrecadados vão para abrigos de crianças em ações sociais.

O coordenador de Promoção Social do Sest Senat, Elton Araújo, explicou que valorizar a cultura do estado é também reconhecer as pessoas que mantém as manifestações culturais vivas no cotididiano:

“Cada manifestação cultural carrega histórias, conhecimentos e formas de expressão que passam de uma geração para outra. O festival cria esse ponto de encontro e permite que diferentes públicos conheçam, vivenciem e valorizem a cultura produzida na nossa região”, explicou.

O nome Dabacuri vem de uma tradição indígena da Amazônia ligada à reunião de pessoas, à troca e à celebração coletiva. Inspirado nesse conceito, o Sest Senat reuniu diferentes manifestações culturais em uma programação aberta à comunidade.

Na sexta-feira (18), o festival começa às 18h com a Academia Dance Moove, que traz danças e ritmos de salão. Logo depois, Márcio Prata apresenta uma sessão de zumba.

Às 20h, o cantor Klinger Júnior canta músicas do boi-bumbá Caprichoso. Às 21h, Luciano Araújo encerra a noite com o boi-bumbá Garantido.

No sábado (19), a programação abre com a quadrilha junina Flor de Liz. Às 19h, é a vez da ciranda Sensação da Raiz. O encerramento fica por conta do cantor de pagode Prata Filho.

Além das apresentações, o festival também conta com uma feira gastronômica nos dois dias, com comidas regionais preparadas e comercializadas por empreendedores locais.

articles.title: Os melhores e os piores shows do Rock in Rio 2026... Os destaques e as decepções do festival | G1
articles.standfirst: Leia as críticas do g1 e veja as listas dos 10 melhores e 5 piores dos Palcos Mundo e Sunset. Os critérios levam em conta relevância, talento de cada artista, a apresentação no festival, reação da plateia, escolha do setlist, execução das músicas e parte técnica da performance.
articles.summary: Leia as críticas do g1 e veja as listas dos 10 melhores e 5 piores dos Palcos Mundo e Sunset. Os critérios levam em conta relevância, talento de cada artista, a apresentação no festival, reação da plateia, escolha do setlist, execução das músicas e parte técnica da performance.
articles.body:
Elton John, Hwasa, Bring Me The Horizon, Péricles, J Balvin Luísa Sonza, Hot Milk, Nelly nos melhores e piores shows do Rock in Rio 2026 — Foto: g1

Após sete dias de diferentes programações, o Rock in Rio 2026 acabou neste domingo (13). Mais de 120 atrações passaram pela Cidade do Rock, do metal ao k-pop, reunindo centenas de milhares de pessoas.

O g1 acompanhou e cobriu todos os shows dos palcos principais: Sunset e Mundo. Abaixo, veja os destaques positivos e negativos desta edição do festival.

As listas foram feitas com base nos reviews do g1 , que fez a cobertura dos principais shows do Rock in Rio. Os critérios levam em conta não só a relevância e talento de cada artista. A apresentação no festival, a reação da plateia, a escolha do setlist, a execução das músicas e a parte técnica da performance também são fatores considerados nos rankings.

Eram oito integrantes no palco e muito a se falar sobre a performance deles, mas é difícil escapar do clichê: no show do Stray Kids, o maior espetáculo veio da plateia.

Em sua segunda vinda ao Brasil, após shows em estádios do Rio e de São Paulo no ano passado, o grupo mostrou suas credenciais para ter se tornado headliner da primeira noite de K-pop da história do Rock in Rio.

Foram recebidos por gritos, cantoria e muitas, muitas dancinhas dos STAYs, codinome dos fãs. Eles retribuem com coreografias precisas no palco, com destaque para a de “Domino”. Com tanta dança, é claro que eles se apoiam em vocais de apoio gravados, mas é fácil notar que há partes cantadas ao vivo, como o trecho de “Ai se eu te pego”, hit na voz de Michel Teló. Leia mais sobre o show do Stray Kids.

No fechamento da primeira noite de Rock in Rio, o Foo Fighters deu aos fãs o que eles esperavam. Foi uma performance segura, fruto de seis vindas anteriores ao Brasil. Aos 57 anos, Dave Grohl provou estar em boa forma como cantor. Quem é fã sabe que a voz dele já deu sinais de desgastes por problemas médicos. Aliás, é provável que o otorrino dele não aprove essa ideia aí de cantar o show inteiro mascando chiclete.

Além de trocas no repertório em relação ao The Town 2023, como as inclusões das baladas “Wheels” e “Marigold”, a maior novidade foi a troca de baterista. Ilan Rubin, correto em sua função, entrou em 2025 após a saída de Josh Freese, que tinha assumido o posto de Hawkins no evento em São Paulo. Como no festival paulistano, "Aurora", do álbum "There Is Nothing Left to Lose" (1999), foi dedicada ao baterista, que tocou no Foo Fighters de 1997 a 2022, quando morreu. A balada era a música favorita dele.

Outro momento emocionante, "Marigold" não estava no setlist de 2023. A música escrita por Grohl apareceu primeiro em "Pocketwatch", disco que ele lançou em 1992 com o projeto Late!. O Nirvana, banda anterior de Grohl, gravou uma versão em 1993, como lado B do single "Heart-Shaped Box". Leia mais sobre o show do Foo Fighters.

Marina Sena finalmente estreou no Rock in Rio, no Palco Sunset, no domingo (13). A artista já tinha passado pelo festival como convidada de Luísa Sonza e até pelo The Town, para cantar Gal Costa; mas só agora, em 2026, ganhou um show para chamar de seu.

Podendo mergulhar em seu próprio repertório, Marina aproveitou para expandir suas “Coisas Naturais”. O disco fala sobre raízes e identidade da cantora, natural de Taiobeiras, no norte de Minas.

O que norteou o show, musical e visualmente, foi essa pegada orgânica: rabeca, violões e percussões soltas, roupas e elementos como se feitos à mão. Leia mais sobre o show de Marina Sena.

Pedro Sampaio abriu a programação de um Palco Mundo do Rock in Rio entupido de gente por todos os lados no sábado (12) com um show que marcou o início de uma nova fase da carreira.

Para quem estava em dias anteriores do festival, deu para notar a diferença com outras atrações que tiveram a missão de abrir o Mundo no mesmo horário (Luísa Sonza, por exemplo) até pelo mar de vipões espremidos nas muretinhas de vidro dos camarotes.

Ao longo do show, ele e os dançarinos brincaram de guerra de travesseiros como numa boa festa do pijama. Plumas e penas voaram por todos os lados durante a batalha. Leia mais sobre o show de Pedro Sampaio.

A banda britânica Jamiroquai estava meio deslocada no line-up do dia de k-pop no Rock in Rio. Nesta segunda vez pelo festival – 15 anos após a última –, o grupo ocupou um espaço peculiar entre as atrações: tocou no Sunset, logo antes do headliner Stray Kids, no Palco Mundo.

Com essa concorrência desleal, as fiéis “stays” (fãs de Stray Kids) ficaram por lá, e o Sunset acabou virando, de modo geral, estacionamento de pais… e alguns filhos. E segundo Zé Ricardo, curador do festival, falou ao g1, essa era a intenção.

A sorte é que um bom groove é atemporal, e até as crianças presentes (por insistência dos pais, provavelmente) estavam dançando. Essa é a fórmula mágica do acid jazz do Jamiroquai, que mescla funk, soul, disco com elementos eletrônicos do house ao hip-hop. Baixo inquieto, percussão apertada, teclas com brilho, e ninguém no público ficou parado. Leia mais sobre o show do Jamiroquai.

Depois de conquistar público e estrelas de diversos gêneros musicais, incluindo bambas da MPB, João Gomes resolveu mostrar que tem a senha até para conquistar um bom espaço no Rock in Rio, abrindo as portas do piseiro e ampliando as do forró no festival.

O artista pernambucano voltou ao festival para cantar ao lado do que chamou de Orquestra Brasileira — uma banda montada especialmente para a apresentação.

Tudo isso dentro do possível no ambiente do festival, claro. A orquestra de frevo acabou se misturando ao som da música pop que tocava em estandes de marca, o que deu uma pequena quebra no Carnaval de João. Mesmo assim, muita gente se reuniu para acompanhar o cortejo e entrou na onda. Leia mais sobre o show de João Gomes.

Quem já foi a algum show de Péricles, já deve ter visto ele inserir no meio de seus sucessos do samba e do pagode a faixa "Stand by Me", da lenda do soul Ben E. King. Mas para sua apresentação no Palco Sunset, do Rock in Rio, nesta segunda-feira (7), o artista fez deste gênero o principal. E único.

Péricles deixou para trás a linha musical que o consagrou, abraçou hits do soul e do R&B norte-americanos e usou o português somente para conversar com o público. Leia mais sobre o show de Péricles.

Praticamente com um CPF para chamar de seu, Oli, o vocalista, fez de um tudo: chamou fã vestido de camisa do Brasil para cantar no palco, surpreendeu a plateia que o acompanha desde o inicinho com músicas do primeiro álbum e até se embananou chamando Rio de Janeiro de São Paulo.

A plateia, devota e provocada pelo cantor, tratou rapidamente de formar o maior número de rodinhas que conseguiu, com direito a sinalizadores de tudo que é cor.

No meio do bate-cabeça, ninguém parecia estar nem aí se o mapa do videogame estava sendo jogado em São Paulo ou no Rio de Janeiro. Leia mais sobre o show do Bring Me The Horizon.

Ao entrar (desfilar, na verdade) no Palco Mundo, Hwasa virou parte da história do Rock in Rio. Afinal, cantou no dia da estreia do k-pop no festival, o que fez dela a primeira artista solo (e primeira mulher) do pop sul-coreano por aqui.

Esses marcos combinam com a identidade da cantora: Hwasa se posiciona como uma popstar firme, desbravadora e até feminista para os moldes do k-pop. A artista, que é integrante do girlgroup Mamamoo, consolidou sua carreira solo ao cantar sobre autoestima, empoderamento e sexualidade sem aquela polidez habitual das idols coreanas.

Deu pra ver isso logo de cara. Hwasa já entrou com a música que leva o nome dela, seguida da enérgica “Chili”. De microfone ligado, deixou claro que é diva pop “old-school”: canta bem, dança muito, tem presença de palco e sensualiza um bocado.

A volta de Elton John ao Brasil, após 11 anos, trouxe grandes hinos românticos e o cantor trajando um terno de paletó amarelo fluorescente e camisa azul-marinho. Em sua terceira vinda ao Rock in Rio e oitava vez no país, Elton se tornou o headliner mais velho da história do festival.

Com um repertório que o fez vender mais de 300 milhões de discos em todo o mundo, Elton passeou pelo melhor do rock radiofônico, com baladas imbatíveis como “I Guess That’s Why They Call It the Blues” e “Goodbye Yellow Brick Road".

Sentir ao vivo o peso desses clássicos ganha outros contornos quando se sabe que Elton desacelerou o ritmo na carreira. Só que ele segue entoando “I’m still standing” e a torcida é para que continue em pé por muito tempo. Leia mais sobre o show de Elton John.

Estreante no Rock in Rio, J Balvin convocou o DJ Pedro Sampaio para subir ao Palco Mundo. Juntos, eles cantaram "Perversa", feat lançado por eles em 2024. Em seguida, Pedro disse que tinha um "presente" para Balvin e chamou Melody para apresentar "Jet ski".

Depois do show do brasileiro, J Balvin tinha a importante missão de manter o clima dançante antes de entregar o espaço para Demi Lovato e Maroon 5. As estrelas ainda se apresentariam ao longo da noite que tinha o “pop mainstream” como veia.

Balvin emendou várias músicas e até conseguiu manter o público animado, embora bem menos engajado do que o de Pedro Sampaio. A presença do DJ brasileiro animou bem mais a plateia. Leia mais sobre o show de J Balvin.

Quem leu o nome do show “Luísa Sonza convida Menescal” pensou que a cantora faria uma homenagem à bossa nova tendo o ícone do estilo com algum destaque. A cantora gaúcha, porém, entregou seu recorrente show pop com um pequeno bloco dedicado à bossa. Seria maldade dizer que o mais intimista da performance foi o público pequeno, o menor dentre as três performances dela no Rock in Rio?

Após mostrar força com duas vezes ao Rock in Rio, Luísa teve problemas nesta segunda (7). O pior deles foi a pouca presença de público. Era fácil chegar na grade. Bastava desviar de uns poucos fãs de Elton John, headliner da noite.

Outro problema foi o som. Ele estava embolado e estourado, com a voz da cantora por vezes escondida em uma massa sonora, principalmente em canções de batidas pesadas como “Motinha 2.0”. Era difícil entender o que ela cantava se você não conhece as letras e não se trata de um problema de dicção. Afinal, ela evoluiu bastante como cantora. Leia sobre o show de Luísa Sonza.

A banda britânica Hot Milk estreou no Rock in Rio em horário privilegiado: foi a penúltima atração do Palco Sunset na sexta (4). Mas um bom horário pode ser mais um fardo que uma vantagem, como a banda comprovou ao encontrar um público modesto – bem menos engajado que horas antes, com Detonautas e Biquini.

“Brasil, cadê vocês, p*rra?”, gritou a vocalista Han Mee, com expressão decepcionada ao entrar no palco.

Foi preciso explicar, didática e repetidamente, que ela queria ver gente, rodinhas punk e alguma resposta. Mas pouco funcionou com a apática galera desta sexta – o que deu certo, foi na marra.

Ficou a frustração, mas a sensação de que eles fizeram tudo o que podiam. Nem todo esforço do mundo salva uma banda que não está no palco certo na hora certa. Leia mais sobre o show do Hot Milk.

Mesmo tentando apostar nas músicas mais pesadas de seu repertório, Colson Baker, nome real do artista de 36 anos, enfrentou uma plateia dividida. No começo, interrompeu o show para acalmar parte do público que o hostilizava.

Fãs de Avenged Sevenfold não morrem de amores por MGK, ao que parece. Meio nervoso, disse que era um cara de Ohio vivendo seu sonho e estava ali para cantar para seus fãs. “Existem dois tipos de música: boa e ruim”, explicou, sem deixar claro a qual das duas se dedicava.

Há momentos acima da média como a performance sóbria de “My ex’s best friend”, a última da noite. Em um festival dominado por emos, faria sentido, mas em uma noite de Rock in Rio voltada ao rock pesado, não funcionou. Leia mais sobre o show do MGK.

No chuvoso terceiro dia de festival, Nelly deixou bem claro que não veio para inventar. Com um DJ e um hype man (rapper de apoio), ele comandou uma festa nostálgica na qual basicamente grita palavras de ordem, rima e canta, trajando uma camisa de basquete da coleção da Nike dedicada a Michael Jordan e a Seleção Brasileira.

Não há banda de apoio, transições bem pensadas entre as músicas ou direção artística para aproveitar bem o mega telão. É como se três amigos subissem ao palco e ligassem uma playlist This is Nelly no estilo karaokê, incluindo o R&B “Just a dream”, de 2010, uma das mais cantadas.

Mesmo com uma performance tão enxuta, a plateia aprovou a ideia, embora não parasse de conversar. O pico da tagarelice vinha quando ele não estava cantando hits dele e de outros: de Michael Jackson e Hall & Oates a Journey. Eram apenas versões curtas com Nelly berrando por cima, como se estivesse cantando em seu chuveiro. Leia mais sobre o show de Nelly.

articles.title: El brillante plano en el US Open con Pierce Brosnan del que todo el mundo habla: un reloj y el papel que le perseguirá toda la vida
articles.standfirst: El actor no se quiso perder el triunfo de Zverev en el último Grand Slam de la temporada
articles.summary: El actor no se quiso perder el triunfo de Zverev en el último Grand Slam de la temporada
articles.body: En 1995 se estrenó en las pantallas de cine la primera película de 007 protagonizada por el actor Pierce Brosnan. Ese mismo año en las pistas de Flushing Meadows de Nueva York, el número 1 del tenis mundial, Pete Sampras, conseguía vencer en lo que sería su tercer US Open, al californiano le quedarían todavía otros dos Abiertos de Estados Unidos por ganar mientras que para el irlandés, su carrera como 007 duraría siete años, los que tardó en rodar ‘GoldenEye’ (1995), ‘El mañana nunca muere’ (1997), ‘El mundo nunca es suficiente’ (1999) y ‘Muere otro día (2002). Pero en esta edición del torneo de Estados Unidos de tenis, el cuarto Gran Slam de la temporada, hemos podido vivir uno de los momentos más simpáticos, graciosos y hasta geniales de esta edición, y no fue precisamente por un movimiento en la pista o por un genial golpe de derecha de algún tenista o por un espectacular revés de alguna de las mujeres que han disputado la final femenina. El momento se ha vivido gracias al realizador de televisión y al cronómetro que marca el tiempo transcurrido en el partido. Es habitual que, durante los partidos, el realizador busque el reloj de tiempo cuando está a punto de cambiar a la hora exacta de partido, o las siguientes, un plano con el reloj en 0:59 y en el momento que cambia a 1:00, el plano se va a la pista y ya sabemos que en ese momento ha transcurrido una hora de partido. Pero, en esta ocasión, el realizador televisivo estuvo ágil, observó a los famosos que había en las gradas y después de descubrir a Brosnan tuvo una genial idea. Enfocó el cronómetro con el partido apenas empezado (un juego a cero marcaba en el marcador) y en el momento en el que este marcaba 0:07 fundió el plano con el del actor viendo el partido en la grada, sutil pero eficaz. Muchos telespectadores se dieron cuenta de la situación y pronto las redes sociales se hicieron eco de esta situación despertando la simpatía entre todos ellos. El partido, finalmente terminó del lado del alemán Zverev, que venció al estadounidense Shelton por tres sets a uno (6-3, 7-6, 6-7,6-2).

articles.title: Sydney Sweeney’s Nude Sports Betting Ad Sparks Backlash Among Female Olympians: “A Kick In The Face To Every Woman”
articles.summary: Sydney Sweeney is no stranger to starring in a controversial ad — and her latest effort has infuriated female athletes, including Olympians. Sweeney posed fo...
articles.body:
Sydney Sweeney is no stranger to starring in a controversial ad — and her latest effort has infuriated female athletes, including Olympians.

Sweeney posed for sports betting company Novig "wearing just sports," meaning she was only covering her modesty with footballs, tennis rackets, and basketball hoops.

The campaign dropped last week, prompting inevitable headlines about the Euphoria star's lack of clothes. But over the weekend, concern was vocalised among female athletes about the sexualization of women's sports.

"I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this," Ariarne Titmus, a four-time Olympic gold medalist for Australia, wrote on Instagram.

"Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is – teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity," she continued. "How do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing?"

Gracie Kramer, an American gymnast, posted a highlight reel of her sporting prowess. "Idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sports looks like," read the caption.

Kramer's post has been liked nearly a million times, including by American diver Kassidy Cook. "This 👏👏👏," the Olympic silver medalist commented on Kramer's post.

Others were inspired by Kramer's post and shared their own highlights reel. "There's so much more to women in sport than how they look. It's about their strength, skill, dedication, resilience, confidence and everything they're capable of achieving," wrote Australian sprinter Bree Rizzo.

British sprinter Amy Hunt used a BBC interview to call out the actress. "Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like," she said after racing at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship. "Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears. This is a beautiful evening."

Skye Nicolson, an Australian World champion boxer, said the backlash was about making a "mockery" of women in sport. "There's a big difference between looking 'sexy' because you do sport compared to using sex to sell 'sport'," she wrote in an Instagram story.

"There is nothing wrong with looking good and doing sport and there's nothing wrong with embracing your femininity while also being a badass athlete."

In a post liked by Florence Pugh among others, UK athlete Lucy Davis wrote : "I don't know wtf Sydney Sweeney was doing, but it's 2026. Stop sexualizing women in sport."

Sweeney and Novig have been approached for comment. Sweeney appeared to respond to the criticism on her own Instagram Stories, posting a series of images of nude sports people, including Serena Williams and Megan Rapinoe.

The controversy follows Sweeney's "great genes/jeans" American Eagle ads , which were criticized for promoting eugenics, with Sweeney intoning: "Genes are passed down from parents to offspring, often determining traits like hair color, personality, and even eye color. My jeans are blue."

articles.body: The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards are set to bring together some of the biggest names and most acclaimed shows in television for one of the industry's most anticipated nights. While the ceremony will take place in Los Angeles on September 14, viewers in India will have to wake up early on September 15 to watch the awards live.This year's ceremony will be hosted by ‘Law & Order: Special Victims Unit’ star Mariska Hargitay and will be available to Indian audiences exclusively on JioHotstar.Hargitay has also recorded a special message for viewers in India ahead of the ceremony. “Namaste India, don't miss television's biggest night. 78th Emmy awards, streaming live only on JioHotstar,” she said in a video shared ahead of the event.When will the Emmy Awards 2026 take place?The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards will be held on Monday, September 14, 2026, at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.Due to the time difference between the United States and India, the ceremony will take place during the early hours of September 15 for Indian viewers.Here are the key timings to keep in mind:Red carpet/pre-show: 4:30 AM ISTMain ceremony: 5:30 AM ISTDate in India: September 15, 2026Streaming platform: JioHotstarThe Television Academy's international viewing information lists JioHotstar as the platform carrying both the pre-show and the main ceremony in India.Where can you watch the Emmys 2026 in India?Viewers in India can stream the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards live on JioHotstar. Those who are unable to watch the ceremony live will also be able to catch it on demand after the event.In the United States, the awards will be broadcast live on NBC, with streaming also available on Peacock. For Indian viewers, the main ceremony begins at 5:30 AM IST on September 15, while the red carpet and pre-show will begin at 4:30 AM IST.Mariska Hargitay to host the 78th EmmysMariska Hargitay will take charge as host of this year's ceremony. Her selection as host brings the ceremony back to a more traditional solo-host format.The 2026 Emmys will honour television productions across several categories, including drama, comedy and limited series, with shows and performances being recognised from the relevant eligibility period.Which shows lead the Emmy nominations in 2026?‘The Pitt’ has emerged as the biggest contender at this year's ceremony with 25 nominations. articles.title: El curioso método de Andreu Buenafuente para evitar las estafas telefónicas: “No me lo estoy inventando”
articles.standfirst: El presentador explica su fórmula y Berto Romero aclara su punto de vista
articles.summary: El presentador explica su fórmula y Berto Romero aclara su punto de vista
articles.body: Nadie en España está exento de recibir todo tipo de intentos de estafas, siendo las telefónicas las más habituales y que provocan inquietud y más de un dolor de cabeza a los ciudadanos de a pie. Ni siquiera los famosos se libran de esto y Andreu Buenafuente, presentador de televisión, ha explicado cómo lidia con este tipo de acciones en las que te intentan engañar para obtener un beneficio económico. El catalán, en el inicio de temporada de ‘Nadie sabe nada’, explicó cuál es su método preferido para evitar estas llamadas o mensajes tan molestos y así escapar de los intentos de estafa que se producen a diario en España. Buenafuente relató que había recibido un mensaje, supuestamente, procedente de una entidad bancaria y que le advertía de que su cuenta iba a ser bloqueada, a menos que accediera al enlace que le compartían y actualizara sus datos. Apenas un día después, la misma entidad le aclaraba que era un intento por comprobar si sus clientes caían en la trampa. Tras ello, el presentador confesó que en ocasiones responde a las llamadas: “No me lo estoy inventando”. Lejos de usar alguna broma o comentario sarcástico, Buenafuente indicó que amenaza a los estafadores con un aviso: haber puesto el caso en manos de las autoridades. A pesar de los elogios de muchos por la decisión del presentador, lo cierto es que Berto Romero destacó en ‘Nadie sabe nada’ que, en realidad, la estrategia de Andreu Buenafuente no sirve de nada. El actor señaló que este tipo de llamadas o mensajes las realizan sistemas informáticos y no una persona real, por lo que una respuesta inmediata de la víctima no tiene efecto. “Yo creo que subestimas al bot, porque le entra la palabra policía y se asusta”, se defendió Buenafuente, que a pesar de todo destacó que lo mejor es seguir el consejo de las autoridades y, además de ignorar llamadas o mensajes, lo más recomendable es trasladar esa información a los especialistas.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Chris Martin: 'Life is beautiful in all its colours, even the darker ones; they're here for a reason,'  words of wisdom shared by the 'Coldplay' artist on struggle, acceptance, growth and resilience
articles.summary: Discover Chris Martin's profound quote about life's beauty, including the darker moments. This article explores his views on struggle, acceptance, growth, and resilience, highlighting how challenges can shape us.
articles.body: Sometimes a simple thought hits differently depending on what someone is going through. Perhaps this is why music and lyrics resonate with people differently. Perhaps this is why artists so easily find their way into our hearts. One such artist is Chris Martin, who has touched lives not just with his musical gems but also with his philosophical prowess. Once, with his words, he urged people not to pretend that everything is fine. There are going to be bad days, disappointments and moments when things don’t work out. That is just part of life.Today's quote of the day by Chris Martin reads, 'Life is beautiful in all its colours, even the darker ones; they're here for a reason.'What does Chris Martin’s quote mean?The quote is attributed to Martin in ‘Coldplay: Live 2012’, the concert documentary connected to the band’s ‘Mylo Xyloto’ tour. The line has been repeated on quote websites and social media many times since, but the documentary is the source generally associated with the quote.The interesting part is Martin’s use of “colours.” Life isn’t just one thing. Some periods are exciting and full of possibilities, while others can feel confusing, painful or completely out of our control.It isn’t necessarily about finding a positive reason behind every bad thing that happens. A person can lose something important, make a mistake or go through a difficult period without immediately knowing what it is supposed to teach them. Sometimes, you only understand an experience after you have had some distance from it.A failed plan can make you rethink what you actually want. A breakup can change how you look at relationships. Even a period where you feel completely stuck can eventually push you to make a change you had been putting off.That doesn’t make the difficult experience easy. It just means it can become part of the person you are later.Why are pain and struggle part of growth?Nobody really grows in a perfectly straight line. We tend to hear the success stories after everything has worked out. What gets less attention are the failed attempts, wrong decisions, awkward stages and moments of doubt that came before them.Pain and struggle can be a part of that process. They can make people question their choices and, sometimes, start again.There also doesn’t have to be a big lesson at the end of every difficult experience. Sometimes, getting through it is enough.Accepting that something is difficult is not the same as giving up on it. People sometimes spend more energy asking why something happened than figuring out what they can do now. That can keep them stuck in the same place.Acceptance can simply mean being honest about how you feel. Maybe you’re disappointed. Maybe you’re angry. Maybe you don’t know what comes next.You don’t have to have everything figured out immediately.People often find out how strong they are only when they have no other choice but to keep going. It could be recovering from a major disappointment, starting over after a failure or getting through a period when everything feels uncertain. Resilience doesn’t always look impressive from the outside. Sometimes, it is just carrying on with your normal day when things inside you feel anything but normal.The difficult moments in life can sometimes show us a strength we didn’t even know we had.Why Chris Martin’s quote matters today?It’s easy to look at other people’s lives and assume they have everything figured out. Social media makes that even easier. You see the holidays, new jobs, relationships and achievements, but rarely the things that went wrong behind the scenes.That’s where Chris Martin’s quote feels quite real. Life is going to have difficult phases, whether we want them to or not. There will be disappointment, uncertainty and days when things simply don’t go the way we planned.Martin isn’t saying people should enjoy going through hard times. His words are more about accepting that those moments are part of life too.You can have a successful career and still struggle. You can be happy and still have bad days. Maybe that is what makes the quote worth remembering. The difficult parts don’t necessarily take away from the good ones. They are simply part of life.Chris Martin’s early life and journey to Coldplay stardomChris Martin was born on March 2, 1977, in Exeter, Devon, England. His interest in music eventually brought him together with Jonny Buckland, Guy Berryman and Will Champion, and the four formed Coldplay.The band went from playing small venues to becoming one of the biggest names in music. Their albums ‘Parachutes’, ‘A Rush of Blood to the Head’, ‘Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends’ and ‘Mylo Xyloto’ helped establish Coldplay as a global act.Martin has spent decades performing in front of huge audiences and writing songs that have become part of people’s lives. But the idea behind this particular quote is much simpler than fame or success.Life can be messy. Some parts are great, some are difficult, and some make sense only much later. And perhaps that is what Martin means when he says even the darker colours are there for a reason.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.standfirst: El presentador volvió a bromear a la hora de contar una de las noticias
articles.summary: El presentador volvió a bromear a la hora de contar una de las noticias
articles.body: Si hablamos del presentador de informativos más carismático, a todos se nos viene a la cabeza un nombre y una cara: Matías Prats. Su manera de dar las noticias y hacer un chiste de aquellas más llamativas, ya forman parte de la historia de la televisión y de nuestros hogares. Chistes y momentos divertidos que llegan cuando menos te lo esperas y que siempre se convierten en viral y en inolvidables. La última vez ha sido este domingo, mientras el presentador explicaba en una noticia el término del fenómeno relacionado con la moda en los hombres y que se ha vuelto viral en redes sociales: pheromone-maxxing. “El último fenómeno viral en las redes sociales se llama pheromone-maxim y no es otra cosa que la moda en los hombres de no lavarse el pelo para resultar, dicen, más atractivos", ha explicado el presentador. Para que los telespectadores entiendan más esta nueva moda, Prats ha continuado con la explicación: "Tiene que ver, así lo aseguran sus seguidores, en conseguir conservar unas supuestas feromonas naturales para aumentar la capacidad de seducción". Descripción que se ha visto obligado a hacer mientras la leía directamente del guión. Una vez ha finalizado y mirando fijamente a cámara, Prats, con ese humor que le caracteriza, ha soltado uno de sus chistes para dar su opinión sobre esta moda: “No me gusta un pelo”. Como era de esperar y cada vez que el presentador lanza alguno de sus chistes en directo, el momento no ha tardado en convertirse en viral en redes sociales y muchos usuarios han comentado la publicación que ya alcanza los 1.400 comentarios. Lo que queda claro es que a la audiencia no le gustaría que Prats dejase de hacer sus chistes durante el informativo.
